You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: AI's Adjustment Deepens as Dollar Weakness Triggers an Asian Asset Repricing

TEXT:
1. Asset Performance Last Week
Global markets diverged last week, with Asian equities outperforming, the U.S. dollar weakening, and technology stocks showing mixed performance. Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index rose 3.5%, leading major global equity markets, driven by record highs among China's four largest banks and growing expectations for further policy support following the Politburo meeting. Copper gained 2.6%, supported by stronger expectations for Chinese demand and a weaker U.S. dollar, while gold rose 1.6% to close at $4138, reclaiming the $4100 level. ETH outperformed the broader crypto market, rising 1.4% after Morgan Stanley launched MSSE, an ETH trust with a 0.14% management fee that includes staking rewards, providing an additional source of institutional demand.
The U.S. dollar was the week's weakest major asset class. The U.S. Dollar Index (DXY) fell 1.3%, while the dollar declined 1.9% against the Japanese yen and 1.5% against the Korean won. The won has now appreciated 7.2% against the dollar in July, making it Asia's best-performing major currency for the month. Oil prices eased modestly, with WTI crude down 0.8% and Brent crude falling 0.9%. South Korea's KOSPI declined 2.1%, pressured by a sharp sell-off in semiconductor stocks after the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index tumbled, briefly triggering a circuit breaker on July 29.
Range-bound trading continues in crypto markets. BTC edged down 0.1%, trading within a $61,400–$66,872 range. U.S. spot BTC ETFs recorded $376 million in net outflows during the week, reversing from seven consecutive days of inflows to four straight days of outflows, largely reflecting a more hawkish Federal Reserve outlook. Following Microsoft's earnings release on July 31, ETFs returned to $49.7 million in net inflows for the day, although this does not yet signal a sustained reversal in fund flows.
2. AI Repricing and a Weaker U.S. Dollar
Sector Rotation: From Extreme Divergence to a Sharp Reversal
Last week saw one of the most pronounced sector divergences since 2020. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 0.5%, while the Nasdaq Composite fell 10% from its June high, entering correction territory. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) declined 20% from its peak, meeting the conventional definition of a bear market. On July 29, a sharp sell-off in technology stocks triggered a broad rotation into defensive sectors, with 53 stocks reaching new all-time highs in a single session. That rotation reversed following Microsoft's earnings release. The company reported EPS of $4.81, well above the consensus estimate of $4.22. Microsoft's shares surged 15.5%, triggering a broad short-covering rally across semiconductor stocks. As a result, the number of stocks hitting new all-time highs in defensive sectors fell sharply from 53 to 21.
We believe this rotation highlights two important structural trends.
First, the market is becoming increasingly selective in how it values AI companies. Microsoft's results demonstrated that heavy AI investment can generate tangible returns, supported by accelerating Azure growth and the first measurable contribution from Copilot. In contrast, Meta exposed a model defined mainly by spending, raising its full-year capital expenditure guidance to $130–145 billion. The era of treating all AI-related companies as a single investment theme is coming to an end.
Second, Hong Kong's four largest banks continued to reach record highs for a second consecutive trading day, even as technology stocks rebounded. Dividend yields of 5%–7% continue to attract capital rotating out of high-growth technology names. At the same time, RMB appreciation has narrowed the valuation gap between A-shares and H-shares, while expectations of further PBOC rate cuts have improved the outlook for banks' net interest margins. Together, these three drivers support a structural investment theme that is largely independent of the AI narrative.
A Weaker U.S. Dollar and Asian Currencies

101 . CFTC positioning data also suggest that bullish consensus on the dollar is beginning to weaken, with speculative positioning shifting against the greenback across all six major currencies.
